title: Trump Administration Weighs $100,000 OPT Fee for International Students After Court Blocks H-1B Levy
excerpt: Days after a federal appeals court struck down the $100,000 H-1B visa fee as an unlawful tax, the administration is considering the same charge on the Optional Practical Training program used by hundreds of thousands of graduates.
body:
• The Trump administration is considering a $100,000 fee on the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program, which allows roughly 419,000 international university graduates to work in the U.S. for up to three years after graduation.
  • The proposal comes days after a federal appeals court in Boston upheld a ruling striking down the administration's $100,000 H-1B visa fee as an unlawful tax Congress never authorized.
  • The OPT fee would more directly target top Silicon Valley and Wall Street firms, which recruit heavily from American universities and later convert employees from student visas to H-1B status.
  • The administration is also separately weighing a $100,000 bond for green card applicants outside the U.S. and broader regulatory changes to the OPT program expected this fall.

A New Front in the $100,000 Fee Strategy

The Trump administration is considering attaching a $100,000 price tag to international students' ability to work in the United States after graduating from American universities, according to the Wall Street Journal, citing people familiar with the matter.

https://x.com/WSJ/status/2082866374796554722

The fee would be attached to the Optional Practical Training program, which allows international university graduates to work for one to three years on their student visas. STEM graduates can work for up to three years under the program. Roughly 419,000 foreign nationals were working on OPT in 2024, the latest year for which data are available.

The proposal is still under discussion at the Department of Homeland Security, and it is unclear whether the White House will sign off. A DHS spokeswoman said in a statement: "No policies should be considered final until formally announced."

Court Blocks the H-1B Fee

The new proposal comes directly on the heels of a significant legal defeat. On July 24, the Boston-based First U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to stay a lower court judge's June 8 ruling that struck down the administration's $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas for highly skilled foreign workers.

U.S. District Judge Leo T. Sorokin had ruled that the fee constituted an unlawful tax that Congress never authorized. The three-judge appellate bench agreed with the 20 Democrat-led states that brought the challenge, writing that "the question here is not whether Congress may delegate the authority in question. It is whether Congress has done so."

"The Trump administration has not explained why that clear standard isn't required in this case."

— First Circuit Court of Appeals ruling

The appeals court also found that the administration failed to show why the plaintiff states would not suffer substantial injury if the stay were granted, noting the government "cursorily assert that the plaintiffs would face 'minimal' harm without developing that argument further."

Why OPT Is the New Target

The pivot from H-1B to OPT is strategic. When the $100,000 H-1B fee was first announced in September 2025, widespread opposition from tech giants led the administration to narrow it to foreign recruits seeking to enter the country. But top Silicon Valley and Wall Street firms generally prefer to recruit international students from American universities and later convert them from student visas to H-1B status — meaning the narrowed H-1B fee largely missed these companies.

An OPT fee would target this recruitment pipeline directly. Companies like JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, and major tech firms are among the most prolific users of OPT, using it as a pathway to identify and retain international talent before sponsoring them for work visas.

It is not yet clear who would be required to pay the fee — the international students themselves, their prospective employers, or the universities. The fee would likely be attached to a new requirement announced earlier this month that requires international students to apply for an extension on their visas to use OPT, ending the previous automatic authorization.

What This Means for Indian Students

Indian nationals make up the largest share of H-1B visa recipients and are among the biggest beneficiaries of OPT, particularly the STEM extension. A $100,000 fee could fundamentally alter the calculus for Indian students considering American universities, where total costs often already exceed $200,000 for undergraduate programs.

The OPT program has been a primary attraction for international students choosing to study in the U.S. Advocates argue that without it, most graduates would be forced to leave immediately after graduation, pushing the skills they gained at American universities to foreign job markets.

Immigration restrictionists have long wanted to target OPT, arguing it allows companies to hire foreign graduates without regulations ensuring they are not being paid less than American-born graduates. Under Trump's first term, senior officials including Stephen Miller argued for abolishing STEM OPT but were overruled by more business-minded members of the administration.

What's Next

DHS is working on a broader regulation to rewrite OPT rules, expected as soon as this fall. The administration is also separately weighing a $100,000 bond for green card applicants outside the U.S., redeemable only after they move to the country and become citizens.

Meanwhile, the appeals court case over the H-1B fee continues. Multiple other lawsuits challenging the fee remain pending in other federal courts. The H-1B program provides 65,000 visas annually for highly skilled foreign workers, with an additional 20,000 reserved for holders of advanced U.S. degrees. Before the proposed increase, employers typically paid between $2,000 and $5,000 in government filing fees.
nri_angle: Indian students and H-1B workers face the most direct impact as the largest beneficiaries of both OPT and H-1B programs, with a potential $100,000 fee threatening to upend the pipeline from American universities to U.S. tech and finance jobs.
